expectations.text: Output defends the paired t-test as statistically defensible for this specific design — 2 conditions, complete data, balanced, one score per person per condition
expectations.evidence: 'A paired t-test is the statistically correct, fully sufficient tool here' — stated at the outset and reinforced throughout with reasoning about difference scores, error terms, and design fit.

expectations.text: Output does NOT insist on MLM as required or validate the collaborator's claim that reviewers will reject a t-test here
expectations.evidence: 'Your collaborator is wrong for this specific design' and 'A well-informed reviewer should not object to a paired t-test here — and if one does, the right response is to show the equivalence, not to switch methods.' No validation of the rejection claim.

expectations.text: Output explains that a paired t-test is mathematically equivalent to a two-level MLM for complete, balanced data — it can state this directly, explain that both test the same within-person contrast, or demonstrate the equivalence without requiring a specific model formula
expectations.evidence: Table entry: 'y ~ condition + (1 | id) — Numerically identical to the paired t-test for your balanced, complete data. Same t, same p, same CI.' Also: 'The paired t-test is a special case of a mixed model.'

expectations.text: Output notes where MLM would genuinely add value: missing data, more than 2 time points, additional covariates, or random slopes with more than one stimulus per condition
expectations.evidence: Explicit bulleted list: 'Missing data,' 'Covariates,' 'More than 2 conditions,' and 'Repeated trials per condition: If each person has multiple observations per condition (not just one), then MLM is necessary.'

expectations.text: Output's tone correctly calibrates — direct answer to the actual question rather than reflexively recommending the more complex method
expectations.evidence: Opens with 'Short answer: Your collaborator is wrong' and maintains a clear, direct stance. Explicitly rejects the reflexive MLM recommendation: 'Running the LMM adds no information, adds a layer of complexity, and forces you to pick a random-effects structure that is either (a) redundant or (b) unidentifiable.'
